entries.09c7a85cd5e3c0af4a9cd7e2abc497b7ab7e765a: <div sID="gen8072" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="8" osisID="2Chr.8" sID="2Chr.8"/> <div eID="gen8072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8073" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8074" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we are told, I. What cities Solomon built, <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.1-2Chr.8.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. What workmen Solomon employed, <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.7-2Chr.8.10">ver. 7-10</reference>. III. What care he took about a proper settlement for his wife, <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.11">ver. 11</reference>. IV. What a good method he put the temple-service into, <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.12-2Chr.8.16">ver. 12-16</reference>. V. What trading he had with foreign countries, <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.17-2Chr.8.18">ver. 17, 18</reference>.
entries.a43de999bd8855a21719ba142fea18c225ae3892: <div eID="gen8074" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8073" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Solomon's Buildings. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 992.)</title> <div sID="gen8075" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And it came to pass at the end of twenty years, wherein Solomon had built the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and his own house, <hi type="super">2</hi> That the cities which Huram had restored to Solomon, Solomon built them, and caused the children of Israel to dwell there. <hi type="super">3</hi> And Solomon went to Hamath-zobah, and prevailed against it. <hi type="super">4</hi> And he built Tadmor in the wilderness, and all the store cities, which he built in Hamath. <hi type="super">5</hi> Also he built Beth-horon the upper, and Beth-horon the nether, fenced cities, with walls, gates, and bars; <hi type="super">6</hi> And Baalath, and all the store cities that Solomon had, and all the chariot cities, and the cities of the horsemen, and all that Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem, and in Lebanon, and throughout all the land of his dominion. <hi type="super">7</hi> <hi type="italic">As for</hi> all the people <hi type="italic">that were</hi> left of the Hittites, and the Amorites, and the Perizzites, and the Hivites, and the Jebusites, which <hi type="italic">were</hi> not of Israel, <hi type="super">8</hi> <hi type="italic">But</hi> of their children, who were left after them in the land, whom the children of Israel consumed not, them did Solomon make to pay tribute until this day. <hi type="super">9</hi> But of the children of Israel did Solomon make no servants for his work; but they <hi type="italic">were</hi> men of war, and chief of his captains, and captains of his chariots and horsemen. <hi type="super">10</hi> And these <hi type="italic">were</hi> the chief of king Solomon's officers, <hi type="italic">even</hi> two hundred and fifty, that bare rule over the people. <hi type="super">11</hi> And Solomon brought up the daughter of Pharaoh out of the city of David unto the house that he had built for her: for he said, My wife shall not dwell in the house of David king of Israel, because <hi type="italic">the places are</hi> holy, whereunto the ark of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath come. <div eID="gen8075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8076" type="x-p"/> This we had <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.10-1Kgs.9.24">1 Kings ix. 10-24</reference>, and therefore shall only observe here, <div eID="gen8076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8077" type="x-p"/> I. Though Solomon was a man of great learning and knowledge, yet he spent his days, not in contemplation, but in action, not in his study, but in his country, in building cities and fortifying them, in a time of peace preparing for a time of war, which is as much a man's business as it is in summer to provide food for winter. <div eID="gen8077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8078" type="x-p"/> II. As he was a man of business himself, and did not consult his own ease, so he employed a great many hands, kept abundance of people to work. It is the interest of a state by all means possible to promote and encourage industry, and to keep its subjects from idleness. A great many strangers there were in Israel, many that remained of the Canaanites; and they were welcome to live there, but not to live and do nothing. The men of Laish, who had no business, were an easy prey to the invaders, <reference osisRef="Judg.18.7">Judg. xviii. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen8078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8079" type="x-p"/> III. When Solomon had begun with building the house of God, and made good work and quick work of that, he prospered in all his undertakings, so that <hi type="italic">he built all that he desired to build,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.6">v. 6</reference>. Those who have a genius for building find that one project draws on another, and the latter must amend and improve the former. Now observe, 1. How the divine providence gratified even Solomon's humour, and gave him success, not only in all that he needed to build and that it was for his advantage to build, but in all that he had a mind to build. So indulgent a Father God is sometimes to the innocent desires of his children that serve him. Thus he pleased Jacob with that promise, <hi type="italic">Joseph shall put his hand on thy eyes.</hi> 2. Solomon knew how to set bounds to his desires. He was not one of those that enlarge them endlessly, and can never be satisfied, but knew when to draw in; for he finished all he desired, and then he desired no more. He did not sit down and fret that he had not more cities to build, as Alexander did that he had not more worlds to conquer, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.5">Hab. ii. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen8079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8080" type="x-p"/> IV. That one reason why Solomon built a palace on purpose for the queen, and removed her and her court to it, was because he thought it by no means proper that she should <hi type="italic">dwell in the house of David</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.8.11">v. 11</reference>), considering that that had been a place of great piety, and perhaps her house was a place of great vanity. She was proselyted, it is likely, to the Jewish religion; but it is a question whether all her servants were. Perhaps they had among them the idols of Egypt, and a great deal of profaneness and debauchery. Now, though Solomon had not zeal and courage enough to suppress and punish what was amiss there, yet he so far consulted the honour of his father's memory that he would not suffer that place to be thus profaned where the ark of God had been and where holy David had prayed many a good prayer and sung many a sweet psalm. Not that all the places where the ark had been were so holy as never to be put to a common use; for then the houses of Abinadab and Obed-edom must have been so. But the place where it had been so long, and had been so publicly attended on, was so venerable that it was not fit to be the place of so much gaiety, not to say iniquity, as was to be found, I fear, in the court that Pharaoh's daughter kept. Note, Between things sacred and things common the ancient landmarks ought to be kept up. It was an outer-court of the temple that was the <hi type="italic">court of the women.</hi>
entries.62bde83962c7dd14e5cc4a7ff13b5cc098f99709: <div eID="gen8080" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Solomon's Devotion. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 992.)</title> <div sID="gen8081" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Then Solomon offered burnt offerings unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> on the altar of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , which he had built before the porch, <hi type="super">13</hi> Even after a certain rate every day, offering according to the commandment of Moses, on the sabbaths, and on the new moons, and on the solemn feasts, three times in the year, <hi type="italic">even</hi> in the feast of unleavened bread, and in the feast of weeks, and in the feast of tabernacles. <hi type="super">14</hi> And he appointed, according to the order of David his father, the courses of the priests to their service, and the Levites to their charges, to praise and minister before the priests, as the duty of every day required: the porters also by their courses at every gate: for so had David the man of God commanded. <hi type="super">15</hi> And they departed not from the commandment of the king unto the priests and Levites concerning any matter, or concerning the treasures. <hi type="super">16</hi> Now all the work of Solomon was prepared unto the day of the foundation of the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and until it was finished. <hi type="italic">So</hi> the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was perfected. <hi type="super">17</hi> Then went Solomon to Ezion-geber, and to Eloth, at the sea side in the land of Edom. <hi type="super">18</hi> And Huram sent him by the hands of his servants ships, and servants that had knowledge of the sea; and they went with the servants of Solomon to Ophir, and took thence four hundred and fifty talents of gold, and brought <hi type="italic">them</hi> to king Solomon. <div eID="gen8081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8082" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Solomon's devotion. The building of the temple was in order to the service of the temple. Whatever cost he was at in rearing the structure, if he had neglected the worship that was to be performed there, it would all have been to no purpose. Assisting the devotion of others will not atone for our own neglects. When Solomon had built the temple, 1. He kept up the holy sacrifices there, according to the law of Moses, <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.12-2Chr.8.13">v. 12, 13</reference>. In vain had the altar been built, and in vain had fire come down from heaven, if sacrifices had not been constantly brought as the food of the altar and the fuel of that fire. There were daily sacrifices, <hi type="italic">a certain rate every day,</hi> as duly as the day came, weekly sacrifices on the sabbath, double to what was offered on other days, monthly sacrifices <hi type="italic">on the new moons,</hi> and yearly sacrifices at the three solemn feasts. Those are spiritual sacrifices that are now required of us, which we are to bring daily and weekly; and it is good to be in a settled method of devotion. 2. He kept up the holy songs there, according to the <hi type="italic">law of David,</hi> who is here called the <hi type="italic">man of God,</hi> as Moses was, because he was both instructed and authorised of God to make these establishments; and Solomon took care to see them observed <hi type="italic">as the duty of every day required,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.14">v. 14</reference>. Solomon, though a wise and great man and the builder of the temple, did not attempt to amend, alter, or add to what the man of God had, in God's name, commanded, but closely adhered to that, and used his authority to have that duly observed; and then <hi type="italic">none departed from the commandment of the king concerning any matter,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.15">v. 15</reference>. He observed God's laws, and then all obeyed his orders. When the service of the temple was put into this good order, then it is said, <hi type="italic">The house of the Lord was perfected,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.16">v. 16</reference>. The work was the main matter, not the place; the temple was unfinished till all this was done. <div eID="gen8082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8083" type="x-p"/> II. Solomon's merchandise. He did himself in person visit the sea-port towns of Eloth and Ezion-geber; for those that deal much in the world will find it their interest, as far as they can, to inspect their affairs themselves and to see with their own eyes, <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.17">v. 17</reference>. Canaan was a rich country, and yet must send to Ophir for gold; the Israelites were a wise and understanding people, and yet must be beholden to the king of Tyre for <hi type="italic">men that had knowledge of the seas,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.18">v. 18</reference>. Yet Canaan was God's peculiar land, and Israel God's peculiar people. This teaches us that grace, and not gold, is the best riches, and acquaintance with God and his law, not with arts and sciences, the best knowledge.  <chapter eID="2Chr.8"/> <div eID="gen8083" type="x-p"/>

entries.e21d56ad0ed05dc3745c4c4d5cf709d9c824cabf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3966"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 8</title> <div sID="gen5723" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.1-2Chr.8.6">2Ch 8:1-6</reference>. Solomon's Buildings.<div eID="gen5723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5724" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3966"/><hi type="bold">2. cities which Huram had restored ... Solomon built them, &c.--</hi>These cities lay in the northwest of Galilee. Though included within the limits of the promised land, they had never been conquered. The right of occupying them Solomon granted to Huram, who, after consideration, refused them as unsuitable to the commercial habits of his subjects (see on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.11">1Ki 9:11</reference>). Solomon, having wrested them from the possession of the Canaanite inhabitants, repaired them and filled them with a colony of Hebrews. <div eID="gen5724" type="x-p"/>
entries.31a2ea982e7d7726ed6941713b2f69cd25cf3556: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3967"/><div sID="gen5725" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3967"/><hi type="bold">3-6. And Solomon went to Hamath-zobah--</hi>Hamath was on the Orontes, in Coele-Syria. Its king, Toi, had been the ally of David; but from the combination, Hamath and Zobah, it would appear that some revolution had taken place which led to the union of these two petty kingdoms of Syria into one. For what cause the resentment of Solomon was provoked against it, we are not informed, but he sent an armed force which reduced it. He made himself master also of Tadmor, the famous Palmyra in the same region. Various other cities along the frontiers of his extended dominions he repaired and fitted up, either to serve as store-places for the furtherance of his commercial enterprises, or to secure his kingdom from foreign invasion (see on <reference osisRef="2Chr.1.14">2Ch 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.15">1Ki 9:15</reference>).<div eID="gen5725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5726" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.7-2Chr.8.11">2Ch 8:7-11</reference>. The Canaanites Made Tributaries. <div eID="gen5726" type="x-p"/>
entries.be81110961778b9ea8b6072c7f9e7934577d4ffd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3968"/><div sID="gen5727" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3968"/><hi type="bold">7. all the people that were left, &c.--</hi>The descendants of the Canaanites who remained in the country were treated as war prisoners, being obliged to "pay tribute or to serve as galley slaves" (<reference osisRef="2Chr.2.18">2Ch 2:18</reference>), while the Israelites were employed in no works but such as were of an honorable character. <div eID="gen5727" type="x-p"/>
entries.2a912bb6f4620c2c93626f8ae19c5d0d83fc1b90: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3969"/><div sID="gen5728" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3969"/><hi type="bold">10. two hundred and fifty that bare rule--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.23">1Ki 9:23</reference>). It is generally agreed that the text of one of these passages is corrupt. <div eID="gen5728" type="x-p"/>
entries.df771acf99cad85533e0aac2628288a3e7fff523: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3970"/><div sID="gen5729" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3970"/><hi type="bold">11. Solomon brought up the daughter of Pharaoh out of the city of David unto the house that he had built for her--</hi>On his marriage with the Egyptian princess at the beginning of his reign, he assigned her a temporary abode in the city of David, that is, Jerusalem, until a suitable palace for his wife had been erected. While that palace was in progress, he himself lodged in the palace of David, but he did not allow her to occupy it, because he felt that she being a heathen proselyte, and having brought from her own country an establishment of heathen maid-servants, there would have been an impropriety in her being domiciled in a mansion which was or had been hallowed by the reception of the ark. It seems she was received on her arrival into his mother's abode (<reference osisRef="Song.3.4">So 3:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.8.2">8:2</reference>).<div eID="gen5729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5730" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.15-2Chr.8.18">2Ch 8:15-18</reference>. Solomon's Festival Sacrifices. <div eID="gen5730" type="x-p"/>
entries.eea250088428831e1e7eac4afcefcf473f01ccf8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3971"/><div sID="gen5731" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3971"/><hi type="bold">15. they departed not from the commandment of the king--</hi>that is, David, in any of his ordinances, which by divine authority he established.<div eID="gen5731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5732" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto the priests and Levites concerning any matter, or concerning the treasures--</hi>either in regulating the courses of the priests and Levites, or in the destination of his accumulated treasures to the construction and adornment of the temple. <div eID="gen5732" type="x-p"/>
entries.c47cb2db81ef4c5b100d51432d697b02a6abbf16: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3972"/><div sID="gen5733" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3972"/><hi type="bold">17. Then went Solomon to Ezion-geber, and to Eloth--</hi>These two maritime ports were situated at the eastern gulf of the Red Sea, now called the Gulf of Akaba. Eloth is seen in the modern Akaba, Ezion-geber in El Gudyan [Robinson]. Solomon, determined to cultivate the arts of peace, was sagacious enough to perceive that his kingdom could become great and glorious only by encouraging a spirit of commercial enterprise among his subjects; and, accordingly, with that in mind he made a contract with Huram for ships and seamen to instruct his people in navigation. <div eID="gen5733" type="x-p"/>
entries.a3add33ffe471763c292567756b081a3cb777d70: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3973"/><div sID="gen5734" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3973"/><hi type="bold">18. Huram sent him ... ships--</hi>either sent him ship-men, able seamen, overland; or, taking the word "sent" in a looser sense, supplied him, that is, built him ships--namely, in docks at Eloth (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.26">1Ki 9:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.27">27</reference>). This navy of Solomon was manned by Tyrians, for Solomon had no seamen capable of performing distant expeditions. The Hebrew fishermen, whose boats plied on the Sea of Tiberias or coasted the shores of the Mediterranean, were not equal to the conducting of large vessels laden with valuable cargoes on long voyages and through the wide and unfrequented ocean.<div eID="gen5734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5735" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">four hundred and fifty talents of gold--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.28">1Ki 9:28</reference>). The text in one of these passages is corrupt. <chapter eID="2Chr.8"/>

entries.aa32f5b45adfc3e2e0e571b743c29820b11465be: <div eID="gen14060" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen14061" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14062" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14062" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14061" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14063" type="x-p"/> Solomon's buildings, conquests, and officers, <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.1-2Chr.8.10">2Chr 8:1-10</reference>. He brings Pharaoh's daughter to his new-built palace, <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.11">2Chr 8:11</reference>. His various sacrifices, and arrangement of the priests, Levites, and porters, <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.12-2Chr.8.16">2Chr 8:12-16</reference>. He sends a fleet to Ophir, <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.17">2Chr 8:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.18">2Chr 8:18</reference>. <div eID="gen14063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14064" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen14064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14065" type="x-p"/> At the end of twenty years - He employed seven years and a half in building the temple, and twelve and a half, or thirteen, in building his own house. - Compare this with <reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.1">1Kgs 7:1</reference>.
entries.b48f40a37d0966ed3faa8f2277108e9f3758f9f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen14065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14066" type="x-p"/> The cities which Huram had restored - See the note on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.11">1Kgs 9:11</reference>.
entries.5c8b35f23617a80202a61387213e98dc4bf703f9: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen14066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14067" type="x-p"/> Hamath-zobah - "Emessa, on the river Orontes." - Calmet.
entries.956c47d16c95fc71da96f4b76a53de7f50b680a3: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen14067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14068" type="x-p"/> Tadmor - Palmyra. See the note on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.18">1Kgs 9:18</reference>, for an account of this superb city.
entries.d29311b9aaec76c3fa3421092d9daea0566ad2d1: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen14068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14069" type="x-p"/> All the store cities - See the note on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.19">1Kgs 9:19</reference>.
entries.c798426d9c0f9c05faebf2cc86ff72418f6b5fac: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen14069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14070" type="x-p"/> But of the children of Israel - See the note on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.21">1Kgs 9:21</reference>.
entries.1392f2318f12e62d88b2a4ce4e14462a19ee6fc1: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen14070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14071" type="x-p"/> The daughter of Pharaoh - "And Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh, Solomon brought up from the city of David to the palace which he had built for her." - T. <div eID="gen14071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14072" type="x-p"/> Because the places are holy - Is not this a proof that he considered his wife to be a heathen, and not proper to dwell in a place which had been sanctified? Solomon had not yet departed from the true God.
entries.33961a0db69566d8f4fefd367197f9fa3a94c096: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen14072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14073" type="x-p"/> Three times in the year - These were the three great annual feasts.
entries.e92527ca4ebd9abf3de51d3300b9b3a7a038fece: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen14073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14074" type="x-p"/> The commandment of the king - The institutions of David.
entries.dbd3dd746d954349b410595efb41a8687eddd639: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen14074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14075" type="x-p"/> Then went Solomon to Ezion-geber - See the notes on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.26-1Kgs.9.28">1Kgs 9:26-28</reference> (note), for conjectures concerning Ezion-geber and Ophir.
entries.1e17aa22a3b8833c721c5ef4f320ddf25400e89d: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen14075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14076" type="x-p"/> Knowledge of the sea - Skilful sailors. Solomon probably bore the expenses and his friend, the Tyrian king, furnished him with expert sailors; for the Jews, at no period of their history, had any skill in maritime affairs, their navigation being confined to the lakes of their own country, from which they could never acquire any nautical skill. The Tyrians, on the contrary, lived on and in the sea.  <chapter eID="2Chr.8"/> <div eID="gen14076" type="x-p"/>

entries.565fbad84ed22651ee39425fa59937a3f422296c: <div eID="gen5959" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Solomon’s City-Building, Statute Labour, Arrangement of Public Worship, and Nautical Undertakings - 2 Chronicles 8</title> <div sID="gen5960" type="x-p"/> The building of the temple was the most important work of Solomon’s reign, as compared with which all the other undertakings of the king fall into the background; and these are consequently only summarily enumerated both in the book of Kings and in the Chronicle. In our chapter, in the first place, we have, (<hi type="italic">a</hi>) the building or completion of various cities, which were of importance partly as strongholds, partly as magazines, for the maintenance of the army necessary for the defence of the kingdom against hostile attacks (<reference osisRef="2Chr.8.1-2Chr.8.6">2Ch 8:1-6</reference>); (<hi type="italic">b</hi>) the arrangement of the statute labour for the execution of all his building works (<reference osisRef="2Chr.8.7-2Chr.8.11">2Ch 8:7-11</reference>); (<hi type="italic">c</hi>) the regulation of the sacrificial service and the public worship (<reference osisRef="2Chr.8.12-2Chr.8.16">2Ch 8:12-16</reference>); and (<hi type="italic">d</hi>) the voyage to Ophir (<reference osisRef="2Chr.8.17">2Ch 8:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.18">2Ch 8:18</reference>). All these undertakings are recounted in the same order and in the same aphoristic way in 1 Kings 9:10-28, but with the addition of various notes, which are not found in our narrative; while the Chronicle, again, mentions several not unimportant though subordinate circumstances, which are not found in the book of Kings; whence it is clear that in the two narratives we have merely short and mutually supplementary extracts from a more elaborate description of these matters. <div eID="gen5960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5961" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.1">2Ch 8:1</reference> <hi type="italic">The city-building</hi>. - 2Ch 8:1. The date, “at the end of twenty years, when Solomon ... had built,” agrees with that in 1Ki 9:10. The twenty years are to be reckoned from the commencement of the building of the temple, for he had spent seven years in the building of the temple, and thirteen years in that of his palace (1Ki 6:38; 1Ki 7:1).
entries.0e4091d3e5bb11042f9ed192cfa2157a74ce3d2b: <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.2-2Chr.8.4">2Ch 8:2-4</reference> <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.2">2Ch 8:2</reference> must be regarded as the apodosis of <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.1">2Ch 8:1</reference>, notwithstanding that the object, the cities which ... precedes. The unusual position of the words is the result of the aphoristic character of the notice. As to its relation to the statement 1Ki 9:10-13, see the discussion on that passage. בּנה, <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.2">2Ch 8:2</reference>, is not to be understood of the fortification of these cities, but of their completion, for, according to 1Ki 9:10, 1Ki 9:13, they were in very bad condition. ויּושׁב, he caused to dwell there, i.e., transplanted Israelites thither, cf. 2Ki 17:6. The account of the cities which Solomon built, i.e., fortified, is introduced (<reference osisRef="2Chr.8.3">2Ch 8:3</reference>) by the important statement, omitted in 1 Kings 9: “Solomon went to Hamath-zobah, and prevailed against it.” על חזק, to be strong upon, that is, prevail against, conquer; cf. 2Ch 27:5. Hamath-zobah is not the city Hamath in Zobah, but, as we learn from <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.4">2Ch 8:4</reference>, the land or kingdom of Hamath. This did not lie, any more than the city Hamath, in Zobah, but bordered on the kingdom of Zobah: cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.3">1Ch 18:3</reference>; and as to the position of Zobah, see the Commentary on 2Sa 8:3. In David’s time Hamath and Zobah had their own kings; and David conquered them, and made their kingdoms tributary (<reference osisRef="1Chr.18.3-1Chr.18.10">1Ch 18:3-10</reference>). Because they bordered on each other, Hamath and Zobah are here bound together as a <hi type="italic">nomen compos</hi>. עליה יחזק signifies at least this, that these tributary kingdoms had either rebelled against Solomon, or at least had made attempts to do so; which Solomon suppressed, and in order to establish his dominion over them fortified Tadmor, i.e., Palmyra, and all the store cities in the land of Hamath (see on 1Ki 9:18.); for, according to 1Ki 11:23., he had Rezon of Zobah as an enemy during his whole reign; see on that passage.
entries.d101ad838ea672791aa3a7ec9d5f551a1a7f758b: <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.5-2Chr.8.6">2Ch 8:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen5961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5962" type="x-p"/> Besides these, he made Upper and Nether Beth-horon (see on <reference osisRef="1Chr.7.24">1Ch 7:24</reference>) into fortified cities, with walls, gates, and bars. מצור ערי is the second object of ויּבן, and וגו חומות is in apposition to that. Further, he fortified Baalah, in the tribe of Dan, to defend the kingdom against the Philistines, and, according to 1Ki 9:15-17, Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer also, - which are omitted here, while in 1Ki 9:17 Upper Beth-horon is omitted, - and store cities, chariot cities, and cavalry cities; see on 1Ki 9:15-19.
entries.bbfc4b68f060247b5e52b6cdee9dc4af3d8f4393: <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.7-2Chr.8.8">2Ch 8:7-8</reference> <hi type="italic">On the arrangement of the statute labour,</hi> see on 1Ki 9:20-23. - This note is in Chr. abruptly introduced immediately after the preceding. <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.7">2Ch 8:7</reference> is an absolute clause: “as regards the whole people, those.” מן־בּניהם (<reference osisRef="2Chr.8.8">2Ch 8:8</reference>) is not partitive: some of their sons; but is only placed before the אשׁר: those of their sons (i.e., of the descendants of the whole Canaanite people) who had remained in the land, whom the Israelites had not exterminated; Solomon made a levy of these for statute labourers. The מן is wanting in 1 Kings, but is not to be struck out here on that account. Much more surprising is the אשׁר after שׂראל מן־בּני, <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.9">2Ch 8:9</reference>, which is likewise not found in 1 Kings, since the following verb נתן לא is not to be taken relatively, but contains the predicate of the subject contained in the words ישׂ מן־בּני. This אשׁר cannot be otherwise justified than by supposing that it is placed after ישׂ בני מן, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.69.27">Psa 69:27</reference> it is placed after the subject of the relative clause, and so stands for ישׂ בני מן בן אשׂר: those who were of the sons of Israel (i.e., Israelites) Solomon did not make ... The preplacing of בּניהם מן in <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.8">2Ch 8:8</reference> would naturally suggest that ישׂ בני מן should also precede, in order to bring out sharply the contrast between the sons of the Canaanites and the sons of Israel.
entries.5db6f21d888a8becf31f3af5acb85d6b7284f5fd: <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.9-2Chr.8.10">2Ch 8:9-10</reference> שׁלישׁיו ושׁרי should be altered into ושׁלישׁיו שׂריו as in 1Ki 9:22, for שׁלישׁים are not chariot combatants, but royal adjutants; see on <reference osisRef="Exod.14.7">Exo 14:7</reference> and 2Sa 23:8. Over the statute labourers 250 upper overseers were placed. נציבים שׂרי, chief of the superiors, i.e., chief overseer. The Keth. נציבים, <hi type="italic">praefecti</hi>, is the true reading; cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.13">1Ch 18:13</reference>; 2Ch 17:2. The <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> has arisen out of 1Ki 9:23. These overseers were Israelites, while in the number 550 (1Ki 9:23) the Israelite and Canaanite upper overseers are both included; see on 2Ch 2:17. בּעם refers to כּל־העם, <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.7">2Ch 8:7</reference>, and denotes the Canaanite people who remained.
entries.1f44301925172a2c32aea51731da94751621a668: <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.11">2Ch 8:11</reference> <div eID="gen5962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5963" type="x-p"/> The remark that Solomon caused Pharaoh’s daughter, whom he had married (1Ki 3:1), to remove from the city of David into the house which he had built her, i.e., into that part of his newly-built palace which was appointed for the queen, is introduced here, as in 1Ki 9:24, because it belongs to the history of Solomon’s buildings, although in the Chronicle it comes in very abruptly, the author not having mentioned Solomon’s marriage to the daughter of Pharaoh (1Ki 3:1). The reason given for this change of residence on the part of the Egyptian princess is, that Solomon could not allow her, an Egyptian, to dwell in the palace of King David, which had been sanctified by the reception of the ark, and consequently assigned to her a dwelling in the city of David until he should have finished the building of his palace, in which she might dwell along with him. המּה is, as neuter, used instead of the singular; cf. Ew. §318, <hi type="italic">b</hi>. See also on 1Ki 3:1 and 1Ki 9:24.
entries.b89da5f6a6c182285aeb5e6bc59060e88445d655: <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.12">2Ch 8:12</reference> <hi type="italic">The sacrificial service in the new temple</hi>. Cf. 1Ki 9:25, where it is merely briefly recorded that Solomon offered sacrifices three times a year on the altar built by him to the Lord. In our verses we have a detailed account of it. אז, at that time, <hi type="italic">scil.</hi> when the temple building had been finished and the temple dedicated (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.1">2Ch 8:1</reference>), Solomon offered burnt-offerings upon the altar which he had built before the porch of the temple. He no longer now sacrifices upon the altar of the tabernacle at Gibeon, as in the beginning of his reign (2Ch 1:3.).
entries.40e3d77a42d03c8686ef868c2e7a777b8b4c397f: <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.13">2Ch 8:13</reference> “Even sacrificing at the daily rate, according to the direction of Moses.” These words give a supplementary and closer definition of the sacrificing in the form of an explanatory subordinate clause, which is interpolated in the principal sentence. For the following words וגו לשּׁבּתות belong to the principal sentence (<reference osisRef="2Chr.8.12">2Ch 8:12</reference>): he offered sacrifices ... on the sabbaths, the new moons, etc. The ו before בּדבר is explicative, and that = viz.; and the infin. להעלות, according to the later usage, instead of infin. absol.; cf. Ew. §280, <hi type="italic">d</hi>. The preposition בּ (before דּבר) is the so-called b essentiae: consisting in the daily (rate) to sacrifice (this); cf. Ew. §299, <hi type="italic">b</hi>. The daily rate, i.e., that which was prescribed in the law of Moses for each day, cf. Lev 23:37. למּועדות is further explained by the succeeding clause: on the three chief festivals of the year.
entries.131e2d7d56e499acbc90a9cf0eefdd6d190ce179: <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.14">2Ch 8:14</reference> <div eID="gen5963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5964" type="x-p"/> He ordered the temple service, also, entirely according to the arrangement introduced by David as to the service of the priests and Levites. He appointed, according to the ordinance of David his father, i.e., according to the ordinance established by David, the classes of the priests (see on 1 Chron 24) to that service, and the Levites to their stations (משׁמרות as in <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.6">2Ch 7:6</reference>), to praise (cf. 1 Chron 25), and to serve before the priests (1Ch 23:28.), according to that which was appointed for every day, and the doorkeepers according to their courses, etc. (see 1 Chron 27:1-19). With the last words cf. Neh 12:24.
entries.cb988278aab24f1f36803b5e46f56713401693d3: <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.15-2Chr.8.16">2Ch 8:15-16</reference> <div eID="gen5964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5965" type="x-p"/> This arrangement was faithfully observed by the priests and Levites. The verb סוּר is here construed <hi type="italic">c. accus</hi>. in the signification to transgress a command (cf. Ew. §282, <hi type="italic">a</hi>), and it is therefore not necessary to alter מצות into ממּצות. על־הכּהנים depends upon מצות: the king’s command concerning the priests and the Levites, i.e., that which David commanded them. וגו לכל־דּבר, in regard to all things, and especially also in regard to the treasures; cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.26.20">1Ch 26:20</reference>-28. - With <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.16">2Ch 8:16</reference> the account of what Solomon did for the public worship is concluded: “Now all the work of Solomon was prepared until the (this) day, the foundation of the house of Jahve until its completion; the house of Jahve was finished.” מלאכת is explained by מוּסד. היּום is the day on which, after the consecration of the completed temple, the regular public worship was commenced in it, which doubtless was done immediately after the dedication of the temple. Only when the regular worship according to the law of Moses, and with the arrangements as to the service of the priests and Levites established by David, had been commenced, was Solomon’s work in connection with the temple completed, and the house of God שׁלם, <hi type="italic">integer</hi>, perfect in all its parts, as it should be. The last clause, בית י שׁלם, is connected rhetorically with what precedes without the conjunction, and is not to be regarded as a subscription, “with which the historian concludes the whole narrative commencing with 2Ch 2:1” (Berth.); for שׁלם does not signify “ended,” or to be at an end, but to be set thoroughly (perfectly) in order.
entries.58b14b36cc6992be263861711481627b37bbcbe4: <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.17-2Chr.8.18">2Ch 8:17-18</reference> <hi type="italic">Voyage to Ophir</hi>. Cf. 1Ki 9:26-28, and the commentary on that passage, where we have discussed the divergences of our narrative, and have also come to the conclusion that Ophir is not to be sought in India, but in Southern Arabia. By אז the date of this voyage is made to fall in the period after the building of the temple and the palace, i.e., in the second half of Solomon’s reign.  <chapter eID="2Chr.8"/> <div eID="gen5965" type="x-p"/>
